claims.text: Applying a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating to MoNbTaTiW RHEA improves its high-temperature oxidation resistance.
MoNbTaTiW has excellent mechanical performance at high temperatures.
Uncoated MoNbTaTiW has limited oxidation resistance during prolonged high-temperature exposure in air.
A Si-20Cr-20Fe coating can be deposited on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method.
The coating should provide protection at approximately 1000–1100°C in air for exposures of 50–200 hours.
Silicon diffuses from the silicide coating during high-temperature oxidation.
Diffusion of silicon and other alloying species produces a continuous, adherent surface oxide/silicide scale.
After oxidation, the coating consists of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer.
The protective scale is compact and comprises SiO2, possibly together with mixed chromium and iron oxides.
The oxide/silicide scale impedes oxygen ingress and thereby limits oxidation of the underlying RHEA.
The coated alloy will have a significantly lower oxidation rate and lower mass gain per unit area than the untreated alloy.
The coated alloy will retain its structural integrity under extreme-temperature conditions better than the untreated alloy.
Untreated MoNbTaTiW forms a non-protective or spalling oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
Oxidation of untreated MoNbTaTiW causes rapid mass gain and degradation.
Performance under thermal cycling or in oxidizing environments other than air is uncertain.
Long-term coating adhesion and mechanical compatibility under repeated thermal cycling require validation.
The proposed experiment compares fused-slurry-coated and uncoated MoNbTaTiW samples after isothermal oxidation at 1000°C in air for 50 hours.
The hypothesis is falsified if coated samples show neither a statistically significant reduction in mass gain nor a continuous, adherent protective scale relative to uncoated controls.
